idiom_name: execute-around helper (withFile(path, body)) or try/finally at the acquisition site; using + Symbol.dispose on engines that implement explicit resource management
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no destructor, no scope-exit statement for plain objects and no deterministic finalization - FinalizationRegistry callbacks run at GC time and cannot be the release point - so the classic owner object is replaced by a callback bracket: one function acquires, runs the body and releases in a finally clause, which executes on every exit path including thrown values. Writing try/finally at each call site works too but repeats the pairing, and an unhandled rejection or a resource acquired in a second branch is exactly how the leak comes back. The syntax-level answer exists in modern engines - the using declaration with Symbol.dispose/Symbol.asyncDispose (explicit resource management) - but MDN still reports it as not Baseline, so a library keeps the callback form as its public API and uses the declaration only where the target runtime provides the symbol.
pitfalls: finally does not await: a promise-returning close inside a non-async finally is fire-and-forget, so async resources need an async function with await in the finally (or await using), otherwise the teardown races the next statement.

The using declaration is not Baseline and requires Symbol.dispose on the value plus runtime support: shipping it to older runtimes without a polyfill throws at the declaration instead of releasing the resource.

Ownership is not in the type: any reference that escapes the bracket keeps working against a closed handle and fails later with EBADF-style errors, so the bracket must stay the only way the handle is handed out.
